flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra ID vs. the old "Azure Active Directory" name
flashcards.back: Microsoft Entra ID is the current name for Azure's cloud identity and access management service, formerly branded Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). The underlying service, tenant model, and APIs are the same — only the product name changed.
flashcards.detail: Current documentation and the exam use "Microsoft Entra ID" exclusively; a distractor still calling it "Azure AD" is testing whether you know it is the same service under a new name, not a different product.

flashcards.front: Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) vs. static token lifetimes
flashcards.back: Continuous Access Evaluation lets Microsoft Entra ID and CAE-enabled services react to critical events in near real time (a user is disabled, a password is changed, a network location changes) by revoking or re-evaluating an access token immediately, instead of waiting for it to naturally expire.
flashcards.detail: Without CAE, a disabled user's existing access token could keep working for its full lifetime (often up to an hour); CAE closes that window by pushing the revocation signal directly to the relying service.

flashcards.front: Cross-tenant access settings vs. workload identity federation
flashcards.back: Cross-tenant access settings control how a Microsoft Entra tenant trusts users signing in from another Entra tenant (inbound/outbound B2B collaboration), including which MFA and device claims are trusted. Workload identity federation lets an external identity provider's token (e.g., a GitHub Actions or Kubernetes service account token) be exchanged for an Entra ID token without storing a client secret or certificate at all.
flashcards.detail: Workload identity federation is the credential-free alternative to a service principal client secret for external CI/CD pipelines — the trust relationship itself replaces the secret, rather than the secret merely being rotated more often.

flashcards.front: Network security group (NSG) vs. application security group (ASG)
flashcards.back: An NSG filters traffic to/from resources using rules based on source/destination IP, port, and protocol, applied to a subnet or NIC. An ASG lets you group VMs by application role (e.g., 'WebServers') and reference that group name in NSG rules instead of hard-coding IP addresses.
flashcards.detail: ASGs make NSG rules easier to maintain as VMs are added or removed from a role, since the rule targets the group rather than a list of IPs that must be updated by hand.

flashcards.front: Azure Firewall Standard vs. Premium
flashcards.back: Azure Firewall Standard provides L3-L7 filtering, FQDN filtering, and threat intelligence-based filtering. Premium adds TLS inspection, IDPS (intrusion detection and prevention), URL filtering, and web category filtering for deeper inspection of encrypted traffic.
flashcards.detail: A scenario asking the firewall to inspect inside TLS-encrypted traffic or detect/block intrusion attempts is pointing specifically at the Premium tier — Standard cannot do TLS inspection or IDPS.

flashcards.front: Azure Bastion
flashcards.back: A fully managed PaaS service that provides secure RDP/SSH connectivity to VMs directly through the Azure portal over TLS, without assigning the VM a public IP address or opening RDP/SSH ports to the internet.
flashcards.detail: Bastion is deployed into its own dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet, and it defeats port scanning specifically because the target VMs never need a public IP at all.

flashcards.front: Private endpoint vs. service endpoint
flashcards.back: A private endpoint assigns a PaaS service (like a storage account or SQL database) a private IP address inside your VNet, so traffic never leaves the Microsoft backbone or the public internet. A service endpoint extends your VNet identity to the service over the Microsoft backbone, but the service still keeps a public endpoint.
flashcards.detail: Private endpoints are the stronger control: because the service gets an actual private IP in your VNet, you can also block all public access to it entirely, which a service endpoint alone does not let you do as cleanly.

flashcards.front: Web Application Firewall (WAF): detection vs. prevention mode
flashcards.back: A WAF (on Application Gateway or Front Door) inspects HTTP(S) requests for common exploits like SQL injection and cross-site scripting using OWASP-based rule sets. Detection mode logs matching requests without blocking them; prevention mode actively blocks matched requests and logs them.
flashcards.detail: Detection mode is the recommended way to test a new WAF policy or ruleset in production first, since prevention mode blocking a legitimate request (a false positive) can break real user traffic immediately.

flashcards.front: DDoS Protection: Basic vs. Standard
flashcards.back: DDoS Protection Basic is automatically enabled at no cost for every Azure resource, providing always-on monitoring and mitigation of common network-layer attacks. DDoS Protection Standard adds tuned, resource-specific mitigation policies, attack analytics/metrics, cost protection, and rapid response team support, applied at the virtual network level.
flashcards.detail: A scenario asking for detailed attack telemetry, cost protection during an attack, or rapid-response support is asking for Standard — Basic provides no visibility beyond basic platform protection.

flashcards.front: Hub-and-spoke topology for centralized security
flashcards.back: A hub VNet holds shared security services (Azure Firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute gateway, Bastion) that spoke VNets peer with and route their traffic through, so security controls and on-premises connectivity are managed in one place rather than duplicated per workload.
flashcards.detail: User-defined routes (UDRs) forcing spoke traffic through the hub firewall are what actually make this pattern secure — VNet peering alone does not force traffic through the hub unless routing is explicitly configured to do so.

flashcards.front: ExpressRoute encryption
flashcards.back: ExpressRoute provides a private connection to Azure over a connectivity provider, but the circuit is not encrypted by default because it does not traverse the public internet. To get encryption in transit, you add IPsec VPN over ExpressRoute (via Microsoft peering) or use MACsec on a direct connection.
flashcards.detail: A common exam trap: assuming ExpressRoute is automatically encrypted because it is "private." Private just means not going over the public internet — it does not by itself mean encrypted.

flashcards.front: Azure Key Vault access model: RBAC permission model vs. vault access policies
flashcards.back: Key Vault access can use the newer Azure RBAC permission model (role assignments at the vault or object level, consistent with other Azure resources) or the legacy vault access policy model (permissions to keys, secrets, and certificates assigned directly on the vault). Microsoft recommends the RBAC model for new vaults.
flashcards.detail: A vault uses one model at a time, not both simultaneously — switching an existing vault to the RBAC permission model replaces its access policies rather than layering on top of them.

flashcards.front: Storage account authorization: access keys vs. SAS vs. Microsoft Entra ID
flashcards.back: Access keys grant full control of the entire storage account and should be tightly restricted. A shared access signature (SAS) grants time-limited, scoped access without exposing the account key. Microsoft Entra ID authorization lets you assign Azure RBAC roles (like Storage Blob Data Reader) to identities for fine-grained, auditable access without any keys at all.
flashcards.detail: Current Microsoft guidance favors Entra ID authorization over SAS or keys wherever possible, since it centralizes and audits access per identity, rather than per shared token or unrotated key.

flashcards.front: Storage account network security: firewall rules and private endpoints
flashcards.back: A storage account firewall can restrict access to specific virtual networks, IP ranges, or allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass it. Combined with a private endpoint, you can disable the storage account's public endpoint entirely so it is reachable only from approved private networks.
flashcards.detail: Enabling "Allow trusted Microsoft services" is what lets services like Azure Backup or Azure Monitor reach a locked-down storage account without opening it to the wider internet.

flashcards.front: Azure SQL: TDE, Always Encrypted, and Dynamic Data Masking
flashcards.back: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) encrypts database files at rest and is on by default, transparent to applications. Always Encrypted keeps sensitive column data encrypted even in memory and query plans, decrypting only on a trusted client — the database engine never sees the plaintext. Dynamic Data Masking obscures sensitive column values in query results for non-privileged users, without changing the stored data.
flashcards.detail: Dynamic Data Masking is not real protection against a determined attacker — it just masks displayed output for lower-privileged users, while the underlying data is unchanged and still readable by anyone with a masking-bypass permission.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for SQL
flashcards.back: A Defender for Cloud plan that adds vulnerability assessment (scanning for misconfigurations and outdated permissions) and advanced threat protection (alerting on anomalous activity like SQL injection or unusual access patterns) for Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, and SQL Server on Azure VMs.
flashcards.detail: Vulnerability assessment and threat detection are two distinct features bundled under the same Defender for SQL plan — scanning for weak configurations and detecting an active SQL injection attempt are both covered by this one plan.

flashcards.front: Server-side encryption (SSE) vs. Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) vs. encryption at host
flashcards.back: SSE encrypts managed disk data at rest by default using platform-managed keys, transparent to the VM OS. ADE encrypts OS/data disk volumes from inside the guest OS using BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux). Encryption at host encrypts data on the host running the VM, covering temp disks and caches that ADE does not.
flashcards.detail: SSE is already on by default, so ADE and encryption at host are about closing specific additional gaps (guest-level control, or temp disk/cache coverage), not 'turning encryption on' from nothing.

flashcards.front: Securing AKS: network policies and Azure Policy for Kubernetes
flashcards.back: Kubernetes network policies restrict pod-to-pod traffic within a cluster. Azure Policy's add-on for AKS enforces cluster-level guardrails, like disallowing privileged containers or requiring specific labels, evaluated against the built-in Azure Policy for Kubernetes initiative.
flashcards.detail: Network policies control what pods can talk to each other; Azure Policy for AKS controls what kinds of resources/configurations are allowed to be deployed at all — they answer different questions and are commonly combined, not substitutes for each other.

flashcards.front: App Service security: managed identity and mutual TLS
flashcards.back: An App Service can use a managed identity to authenticate to other Azure services (like Key Vault) without storing credentials in app settings. TLS/SSL bindings enforce HTTPS for inbound traffic, and mutual TLS (client certificates) can be required so the app also verifies the identity of the calling client.
flashcards.detail: "HTTPS Only" forces any plain HTTP request to redirect to HTTPS, but it does not by itself require or validate client certificates — that additional verification is what mutual TLS adds.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Foundry agent identity and least-privilege permission scoping
flashcards.back: Every agent built and deployed in Microsoft Foundry runs under its own identity rather than borrowing the developer's or a shared service's credentials, and should be granted only the specific data sources, tools, and downstream APIs it needs to complete its task, following the same least-privilege principle applied to any other workload identity.
flashcards.detail: A Foundry agent granted broad, unscoped permissions 'just in case' becomes a high-value target: a single prompt injection or jailbreak against that agent can then reach everything the over-provisioned identity was allowed to touch.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Entra Agent ID: identity for non-human, agentic workloads
flashcards.back: Microsoft Entra Agent ID gives an AI agent its own individually identifiable, policy-controlled identity, distinct from a human user, a traditional app registration, or a generic shared service principal, so the agent's actions can be authenticated, authorized, governed, and audited on their own — including through its full lifecycle from creation to retirement.
flashcards.detail: Agent identity blueprints act as templates: permissions and Conditional Access policies applied at the blueprint level automatically apply to every agent identity created from it, letting an organization govern a whole fleet of agents through one policy instead of configuring each agent individually.

flashcards.front: Applying Conditional Access to Microsoft Entra Agent ID
flashcards.back: Conditional Access policies can target agent identities the same way they target user identities — requiring conditions to be met (like a trusted network or an approved calling application) before an agent identity is allowed to authenticate and act, extending Zero Trust principles to non-human, agentic identities rather than exempting them from evaluation.
flashcards.detail: Treating agent identities as automatically trusted simply because they are not human is exactly the gap Conditional Access for Agent ID is meant to close — an agent identity with excessive standing access is just as dangerous as an over-privileged user account, arguably more so given how quickly an agent can act.

flashcards.front: Foundry AI Gateway (Azure API Management in front of Microsoft Foundry)
flashcards.back: Deploying Azure API Management as an AI Gateway in front of Microsoft Foundry gives a central control point for agent and model traffic — enforcing authentication, rate limiting/token quotas, logging, and routing policies before a request ever reaches the underlying Foundry agent or model deployment.
flashcards.detail: Centralizing traffic through the gateway is what makes consistent, org-wide policies (like blocking a specific model version or capping token spend per team) enforceable in one place, rather than relying on every agent or application to independently implement the same controls.

flashcards.front: Blast radius analysis for a compromised Entra Agent ID (Defender XDR)
flashcards.back: When Microsoft Defender XDR flags a suspicious or compromised agent identity, blast radius analysis maps out everything that agent identity could reach or had recently accessed — data sources, downstream APIs, other agents it can invoke — so responders can scope containment and cleanup to what the agent could actually touch, not just the agent itself.
flashcards.detail: This is the agentic-identity equivalent of asking 'what could a compromised user account have accessed' — except an agent's permitted actions and integrations often need to be mapped explicitly, since an agent's effective reach is not always obvious just from reading its role assignment.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Copilot data access scope and the oversharing risk
flashcards.back: Microsoft 365 Copilot only surfaces content the requesting user already has permission to see, respecting existing SharePoint, OneDrive, and Microsoft 365 permissions — but if those underlying permissions are already too broad (e.g., a site shared with 'Everyone'), Copilot can now surface that overshared content far more easily and quickly than a human manually searching for it.
flashcards.detail: Copilot does not introduce a new permission model of its own; it inherits whatever access already exists. The real fix for Copilot oversharing risk is remediating the underlying overpermissive SharePoint/OneDrive sharing, not restricting Copilot itself.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Purview DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot
flashcards.back: Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention policies can be applied directly to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Chat prompts and responses, blocking Copilot from using or surfacing content that matches a sensitive information type or label, including preventing that sensitive content from being used in an external web-grounded response.
flashcards.detail: This closes a gap that content permissions alone do not: even a user who is technically permitted to see a sensitive file might still be blocked from having Copilot summarize or quote from it directly, if a DLP policy specifically restricts that AI-generated exposure.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Copilot Studio: real-time protection and admin controls
flashcards.back: Administrators can enable real-time protection for custom agents built in Copilot Studio, which evaluates prompts and responses against configured security and compliance policies as the agent runs, alongside admin controls that govern which connectors, data sources, and publishing channels a maker is allowed to use.
flashcards.detail: Without admin governance over Copilot Studio, individual makers could publish an agent that connects to an unapproved external data source or exposes it through an ungoverned channel — the admin controls exist specifically to keep maker-built agents inside organizational guardrails.

flashcards.front: AI workload data protection: grounding, training, and prompt data
flashcards.back: Data used to ground an AI agent's responses (retrieved documents, search indexes) and the prompts/responses exchanged with it need the same at-rest and in-transit encryption, access control, and retention treatment as any other sensitive data — plus consideration of whether that data could be retained, logged, or used to improve a model beyond the immediate request.
flashcards.detail: A grounding data store (like a vector index built from confidential documents) is a full sensitive-data asset in its own right and needs its own access controls — access to the AI agent's chat interface is not, by itself, a substitute for securing the underlying data store the agent draws from.

flashcards.front: Governance and compliance considerations for AI in Azure
flashcards.back: Beyond technical controls, deploying AI agents and Copilot at scale raises governance questions Azure security teams must own: maintaining an inventory of deployed agents and their owners, auditing agent actions for compliance review, applying data residency and retention requirements to AI-processed data, and ensuring responsible-AI review before an agent is given broader autonomy or access.
flashcards.detail: An agent inventory answers a question that is otherwise easy to lose track of as agent creation gets easier: exactly how many agents exist, what each one can access, and who is accountable for it — the same discipline already expected for human accounts and app registrations.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Secure Score
flashcards.back: A percentage score that aggregates how many recommended security controls an environment has actually implemented, weighted by each recommendation's potential impact. Improving secure score means resolving the underlying recommendations, not the score itself.
flashcards.detail: Secure Score is a prioritization tool, not a compliance certification — a high score reflects following Microsoft's general best-practice recommendations, which is different from passing a specific named regulatory standard.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans
flashcards.back: Defender for Cloud's free tier covers basic posture management (recommendations, secure score). Enabling specific paid Defender plans per resource type (Servers, Storage, SQL, Containers, Key Vault, App Service, Resource Manager) adds workload-specific threat detection and advanced capabilities for that resource type.
flashcards.detail: Plans are enabled independently per resource type at the subscription level — enabling Defender for Storage does not also enable Defender for SQL, so a scenario needing threat detection on both requires enabling both plans explicitly. DNS threat detection is no longer a separate standalone plan for new subscriptions — it now comes bundled into Defender for Servers Plan 2.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access
flashcards.back: A Defender for Cloud feature that locks down a VM's management ports (like RDP/SSH) by default, only opening them for a specific requester, source IP, and time window when access is explicitly requested and approved.
flashcards.detail: JIT reduces the attack surface of exposed management ports without requiring Bastion — but Bastion removes the need for a public IP entirely, while JIT still allows temporary direct access to a port that could carry a public IP if one exists.

flashcards.front: Adaptive application controls
flashcards.back: A Defender for Cloud feature that uses machine learning to build an allowlist of known-safe applications for a group of VMs, then alerts (or can enforce) when an application outside that allowlist attempts to run.
flashcards.detail: This is application allowlisting delivered as a managed, ML-driven recommendation rather than something manually enumerated application-by-application, which is what distinguishes it from a hand-configured allowlist policy.

flashcards.front: Regulatory compliance dashboard
flashcards.back: A Defender for Cloud feature that maps your environment against specific regulatory or industry standards (like PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST), showing which controls pass, fail, or are not applicable, and lets you add custom standards.
flashcards.detail: This is distinct from Secure Score: Secure Score reflects general best practice, while the compliance dashboard reflects standing against a specific named standard an organization may be contractually or legally required to meet.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Sentinel data connectors
flashcards.back: Data connectors ingest log and event data from sources — Azure services, Microsoft 365, on-premises systems, and third-party/multicloud platforms — into the Log Analytics workspace that backs a Sentinel instance, where it becomes queryable and can drive analytics rules.
flashcards.detail: Sentinel has no data to analyze without connectors ingesting logs first — connecting a source is always the prerequisite step before writing an analytics rule or hunting query against that data.

flashcards.front: Sentinel analytics rules: scheduled vs. near-real-time vs. Fusion
flashcards.back: Scheduled analytics rules run a KQL query on a set interval and generate an incident on matches. Near-real-time (NRT) rules run continuously for faster detection on a narrower set of supported queries. Fusion uses machine learning to correlate multiple low-fidelity signals across different sources into a single, higher-confidence incident.
flashcards.detail: Fusion's value is correlating otherwise-unremarkable individual alerts (e.g., an odd sign-in plus an unusual resource deployment) into one incident reflecting a likely multi-stage attack, which a single scheduled rule looking at one data source alone would not catch.

flashcards.front: Sentinel incidents vs. workbooks vs. hunting queries
flashcards.back: An incident is a case created from one or more triggered alerts, grouping related evidence for investigation. A workbook is an interactive visualization/report built from the underlying data. A hunting query is a proactive, manually run KQL search for threats that have not yet triggered any analytics rule or incident.
flashcards.detail: Hunting is explicitly proactive — you run a hunting query looking for evidence of compromise before any confirmed incident exists, as opposed to investigating an incident that already exists because a rule fired.

flashcards.front: Sentinel playbooks (SOAR)
flashcards.back: A playbook is a Logic App triggered automatically from an analytics rule or incident (or run manually) to orchestrate an automated response, like disabling a user account, isolating a VM, or posting a notification to a Teams channel.
flashcards.detail: Playbooks are what turn Sentinel from a detection tool into a SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platform — detection without a playbook still requires a human to take the remediation action manually.

flashcards.front: Log Analytics workspace and KQL
flashcards.back: A Log Analytics workspace is the storage and query backend that both Azure Monitor and Microsoft Sentinel are built on. Kusto Query Language (KQL) is the query language used to search, filter, and analyze the log data stored there.
flashcards.detail: Sentinel does not have its own separate log store — it is deployed onto (and queries) a Log Analytics workspace, which is why enabling Sentinel on a workspace that already collects other Azure Monitor logs makes that data available to Sentinel too.

flashcards.front: Azure Monitor alerts and action groups
flashcards.back: An Azure Monitor alert rule evaluates a signal (metric, log query, or activity log event) against a condition and fires when met. An action group defines what happens when an alert fires — email, SMS, webhook, Azure Function, Logic App, and more — decoupled from the alert rule so the same action group can be reused across many rules.
flashcards.detail: Separating the alert condition from the action group means updating who gets notified (e.g., a new on-call engineer) only requires editing the action group once, not every alert rule that references it.

flashcards.front: Connecting hybrid and multicloud resources to Defender for Cloud
flashcards.back: Defender for Cloud can extend coverage beyond Azure using Azure Arc (for on-premises/other-cloud servers) and native multicloud connectors for AWS and GCP, bringing their workloads under the same recommendations, secure score, and Defender plans.
flashcards.detail: Without Arc onboarding first, an on-premises or AWS/GCP VM has no Azure resource identity for Defender for Cloud to evaluate at all — the connector/Arc step is what makes it visible to Defender for Cloud in the first place.

flashcards.front: Managed identity: system-assigned vs. user-assigned
flashcards.back: A system-assigned managed identity is tied to one resource’s lifecycle, created and deleted with it. A user-assigned managed identity is a standalone resource that can be attached to multiple resources at once and outlives any single one of them.
flashcards.detail: App Service security using managed identity to reach Key Vault or SQL without a stored secret is the classic case this exists to solve — the credential simply isn’t something a developer ever sees or manages.

flashcards.front: Zero Trust principles
flashcards.back: Verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, and assume breach — treating every request as coming from an untrusted network regardless of where it originates, rather than trusting anything just because it’s "inside the perimeter."
flashcards.detail: Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) vs. static token lifetimes and Just-in-time (JIT) VM access are both concrete implementations of "assume breach" and "least privilege" in practice, not abstract ideas on their own.

flashcards.front: Customer-managed keys (CMK) vs. Microsoft-managed keys
flashcards.back: By default, Azure encrypts data at rest with Microsoft-managed keys, with no setup required. Customer-managed keys let an organization supply and control its own key, stored in Azure Key Vault access model: RBAC permission model vs. vault access policies, for scenarios needing direct control over key rotation and revocation.
flashcards.detail: Revoking or deleting a customer-managed key immediately makes the encrypted data inaccessible — a powerful compliance control, but also a real operational risk if the key is lost without a proper backup.

flashcards.front: Confidential computing
flashcards.back: Encrypts data while it is actively in use in memory, inside a hardware-backed trusted execution environment, protecting it even from a privileged administrator or the cloud provider’s own infrastructure — not just data at rest or in transit.
flashcards.detail: This closes the one gap that server-side encryption (SSE) vs. Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) vs. encryption at host don't: none of those protect data while it's actually being processed in memory.

flashcards.front: Workbooks in Microsoft Sentinel
flashcards.back: Interactive, customizable reports built from KQL queries against Sentinel data connectors, used for ongoing operational visibility (like tracking a specific threat category over time) rather than one-off investigation.
flashcards.detail: A workbook is a dashboard you keep coming back to; a Sentinel analytics rules: scheduled vs. near-real-time vs. Fusion detection is a one-time evaluation that fires an alert when its condition is met.

flashcards.front: Entitlement management: access packages
flashcards.back: A bundle of resources — group membership, Teams, enterprise apps, SharePoint sites — that a user can request access to as one unit, going through an approval workflow, rather than an admin granting each resource separately.
flashcards.detail: This is the request-and-approval side of access; Privileged Identity Management (PIM) covers the separate, time-bound activation of privileged roles rather than standing access to resources like these.

flashcards.front: PIM for Azure resource roles
flashcards.back: PIM for Azure resource roles applies the same eligible-vs-active, time-bound activation model used for Entra directory roles to Azure RBAC roles like Owner or Contributor at a subscription or resource group scope, requiring justification (and optionally approval) before the role becomes active.
flashcards.detail: This is a different control from just-in-time (JIT) VM access: PIM governs who can act with a management-plane role at all, while JIT VM access only narrows which source IPs and ports can reach a VM once someone already has network access.

flashcards.front: Sentinel automation rules
flashcards.back: Automation rules run centrally across one or more analytics rules before any playbook fires, letting an analyst auto-assign, tag, suppress, or close incidents based on simple conditions, then optionally hand off to one or more Sentinel playbooks (SOAR) for the actual remediation actions.
flashcards.detail: Ordering matters: automation rules execute in a defined sequence, and a rule that closes an incident outright can prevent a later rule — or a playbook — further down that sequence from ever running against it.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Cloud DevOps security
flashcards.back: Defender for Cloud's DevOps security connects source-control platforms (GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab) to scan for exposed secrets, misconfigured pipelines, and vulnerable dependencies before code ever reaches a running Azure resource.
flashcards.detail: This extends Zero Trust principles upstream of runtime: instead of only assuming breach and verifying explicitly once a workload is already live, it catches a hardcoded credential or an insecure pipeline setting at the source before it can ever be exploited.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Defender for Cloud attack path analysis
flashcards.back: Attack path analysis uses the cloud security graph to identify exploitable chains — like an internet-facing VM with a vulnerability that has a role assignment reaching a storage account holding sensitive data — and ranks them by real exploitability, not just individual finding severity.
flashcards.detail: This is what separates it from the regulatory compliance dashboard: that dashboard checks configuration against a named standard in isolation, while attack path analysis specifically models whether findings chain together into an actual reachable path to something valuable.

questions.question: A security team just disabled a Microsoft Entra ID account after confirming its credentials were compromised, but the attacker still has an already-issued access token that would otherwise remain valid for up to another hour. What should be enabled so relying services revoke that token immediately instead of waiting for it to expire?
options: A stricter Conditional Access sign-in frequency setting
Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)
A shorter static access token lifetime policy
Microsoft Entra ID Protection user risk remediation
questions.explanation: Continuous Access Evaluation pushes critical events, like an account being disabled, directly to CAE-enabled relying services in near real time, revoking the token immediately rather than waiting for its natural expiration. A shorter static token lifetime only narrows the exposure window in advance, it does not react to this specific event after the fact, and sign-in frequency and ID Protection risk remediation govern future sign-ins, not an already-issued token.

questions.question: An organization wants to block sign-ins to a finance application from a specific country and require a compliant device for sign-ins from personal devices, but only for members of the Finance group. Which feature configures this?
options: A Conditional Access policy scoped to the Finance group with location and device compliance conditions
An Azure RBAC deny assignment scoped directly to the finance application's resource group
A PIM eligible assignment granting the Finance group temporary elevated access to the application
A network security group rule on the app's subnet restricting inbound traffic by source country range
questions.explanation: Conditional Access policies combine conditions (group membership, sign-in location) with grant controls (requiring device compliance) scoped to a specific application. NSGs filter network traffic by IP/port with no identity or app sign-in awareness, and PIM governs privileged role activation, not general application access.

questions.question: An Azure Function needs to read secrets from Key Vault, and the security team wants no credentials stored anywhere in code or application settings. What should be configured?
options: A shared access signature scoped to the Key Vault
A service principal with a client secret stored in application settings
An access policy granting the Contributor role on the Key Vault resource
A managed identity assigned to the Function, granted access via RBAC or a vault access policy
questions.explanation: A managed identity lets the Function authenticate to Key Vault using Azure-managed credentials that are never stored anywhere accessible to a developer. Storing a client secret in app settings is exactly the credential-storage risk a managed identity avoids, and Key Vault has no concept of a SAS token for secret access.

questions.question: An administrator who holds the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID reports being unable to modify Azure RBAC role assignments on a subscription. What is the most likely reason, and what fixes it?
options: PIM must first be used to activate an eligible assignment for that role, if the admin has one configured for Azure resource management
The admin must explicitly elevate access to manage Azure resources, since Entra ID directory roles do not grant Azure RBAC permissions by default
Global Administrator lost its Azure RBAC-related capabilities in a recent platform update and now requires a separate custom role
Azure RBAC assignments on a subscription can only be changed by whoever originally created that subscription
questions.explanation: Entra ID directory roles and Azure RBAC roles are separate authorization systems — holding Global Administrator does not itself grant RBAC rights on Azure resources. The fix is the explicit "Access management for Azure resources" elevation setting in Entra ID properties, not a PIM activation for a role that may not even exist for this admin.

questions.question: Guest users from a partner organization need to request access to a bundle of resources — a group, a SharePoint site, and an app — through one approval workflow, with access automatically expiring after 90 days. Which feature fits best?
options: A Conditional Access policy scoped to external users
An access review scheduled quarterly
A dynamic group scoped to the partner's email domain
An access package in entitlement management
questions.explanation: Access packages in entitlement management bundle multiple resources into a single request-and-approval workflow with a defined expiration. Access reviews check whether existing access should continue rather than granting new bundled access, and Conditional Access controls sign-in conditions, not what a user can request.

questions.question: A user account is disabled in Microsoft Entra ID, but the user still holds an active access token for a CAE-enabled application issued 20 minutes earlier. What happens under Continuous Access Evaluation?
options: The token remains valid until its original expiration time, since CAE only applies to new sign-in attempts
The application must be manually restarted before it will recognize the disabled account
The application receives a near-real-time signal and revokes the token, blocking further use almost immediately
The token is automatically converted into a refresh token with an extended lifetime
questions.explanation: Continuous Access Evaluation is designed exactly for this case — a critical event like disabling an account is pushed to CAE-enabled services in near real time, so the existing token is revoked well before its original expiration rather than continuing to work until it naturally expires.

questions.question: A partner organization's users need to sign in to a shared application using their own organization's Microsoft Entra credentials, with specific rules about which of the partner's MFA and device compliance claims should be trusted. Which feature configures this?
options: A dynamic security group scoped to the partner's domain
Cross-tenant access settings, configured for inbound B2B collaboration with the partner tenant
Workload identity federation with the partner's identity provider
A PIM eligible assignment scoped to the partner's users
questions.explanation: Cross-tenant access settings are exactly where an organization defines how much it trusts another Entra tenant's own MFA and device claims for inbound B2B collaboration. Workload identity federation is for non-human workloads exchanging tokens with an external IdP, not human partner sign-ins, and PIM/dynamic groups do not configure inter-tenant trust.

questions.question: A security team needs a firewall that can inspect inside TLS-encrypted web traffic and provide intrusion detection and prevention signatures, in addition to standard FQDN and network filtering. Which option meets this?
options: Azure Firewall Premium
Azure Firewall Standard with a static public IP
A Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway in detection mode
Network security group rules referencing FQDN tags
questions.explanation: TLS inspection and IDPS are Premium-tier-only Azure Firewall capabilities; Standard offers neither. A WAF operates at the HTTP layer for web apps specifically, and NSGs cannot inspect TLS content or provide IDPS signatures at all.

questions.question: Administrators need to RDP into VMs from the Azure portal without any VM having a public IP address or inbound RDP opened on the VNet. Which service should be deployed?
options: A VPN gateway with point-to-site configuration for every administrator
Just-in-time VM access alone, keeping the VMs on their existing public IPs
Azure Bastion, deployed into a dedicated AzureBastionSubnet
An NSG rule allowing RDP only from the corporate office IP range
questions.explanation: Azure Bastion is built specifically to provide portal-based RDP/SSH over TLS without the target VM needing a public IP at all. JIT access still assumes a port on a potentially public IP is opened temporarily, and an NSG rule restricting RDP by source IP still requires RDP to be reachable on some IP, which Bastion avoids entirely.

questions.question: An organization wants traffic to its Azure SQL Database to travel entirely over the Microsoft backbone with a private IP in their VNet, and wants to fully disable the database's public endpoint. What should they configure?
options: A service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql on the application subnet, which also disables the database's public endpoint
A private endpoint for the SQL Database, then disable public network access
An NSG rule blocking all inbound traffic to the database's public endpoint except from the app subnet
A virtual network gateway with force tunneling enabled, routing all traffic through the on-premises private network
questions.explanation: Only a private endpoint gives the database an actual private IP in the VNet, which is the prerequisite for safely disabling its public endpoint entirely. A service endpoint keeps the database's public endpoint in place and only extends VNet identity to it, so public access could still be reachable.

questions.question: A website published through Azure Front Door needs to detect and block common web exploits like SQL injection before they reach the backend. Which control should be applied?
options: A Web Application Firewall policy in prevention mode attached to the Front Door profile
A network security group on the backend App Service's subnet
Azure Firewall Premium deployed in front of Front Door
DDoS Protection Standard on the Front Door profile
questions.explanation: WAF policies specifically inspect HTTP(S) requests for OWASP-category exploits like SQL injection, and prevention mode actively blocks matches. DDoS Protection defends against volumetric/protocol attacks rather than HTTP-layer exploits, and NSGs filter by IP/port with no awareness of HTTP request content.

questions.question: A company connects to Azure over an ExpressRoute circuit and assumes the traffic is automatically encrypted because it never touches the public internet. What is the accurate statement a security review should correct this with?
options: ExpressRoute traffic is encrypted by default using IPsec, the same as a site-to-site VPN connection
ExpressRoute can reach on-premises resources but has no supported path to Azure PaaS services like Storage or SQL
ExpressRoute only carries encrypted traffic when Azure Bastion is deployed alongside it as a TLS termination point
ExpressRoute is private but not encrypted by default; IPsec VPN over ExpressRoute or MACsec must be added for encryption in transit
questions.explanation: "Private" and "encrypted" are different properties — ExpressRoute provides the former but not the latter unless IPsec VPN over ExpressRoute or MACsec is explicitly added. ExpressRoute can also reach Azure PaaS services via Microsoft peering, so that claim is separately wrong too.

questions.question: A hub-and-spoke design places Azure Firewall in the hub VNet, and the team wants all outbound internet traffic from every spoke to be inspected by that firewall. Peering between the hub and each spoke is already configured. What else is required?
options: Nothing further — VNet peering automatically routes all spoke traffic through the hub
User-defined routes (UDRs) in each spoke directing 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the firewall's private IP
A site-to-site VPN connection between each spoke and the hub
Enabling DDoS Protection Standard on each spoke VNet
questions.explanation: VNet peering only enables connectivity between VNets — it does not force traffic through a specific path. A user-defined route sending default (0.0.0.0/0) traffic to the firewall's internal IP is what actually forces spoke traffic through the hub for inspection.

questions.question: A team wants an NSG rule to target VMs by their application role rather than their individual IP addresses, and wants the rule to stay valid automatically as VMs are added or removed from that role. What should be used?
options: A service tag for the Azure region
A list of the VMs' current private IP addresses, updated manually as needed
An application security group (ASG) containing the relevant VMs' NICs
A user-defined route referencing each VM's resource ID
questions.explanation: An ASG lets an NSG rule reference a named group of VM NICs by application role, and membership automatically stays current as VMs are added or removed — no rule update needed when VM IPs change. A static IP list requires manual maintenance, which defeats the stated goal.

questions.question: A compliance requirement states that sensitive columns in an Azure SQL Database must remain encrypted even from database administrators and the database engine itself, decrypting only inside a trusted client application. Which feature meets this?
options: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)
Dynamic Data Masking
Azure Disk Encryption on the underlying storage
Always Encrypted
questions.explanation: Always Encrypted keeps data encrypted in memory and in query plans, decrypting only on a trusted client driver — the database engine (and therefore a DBA) never sees the plaintext. TDE only protects data at rest on disk, and Dynamic Data Masking merely obscures displayed values without changing how the data is stored or processed.

questions.question: A storage account currently allows access only through its account access keys, which are shared among several applications and grant unrestricted full control. What is the recommended remediation?
options: Rotate the access keys weekly instead of changing the authorization model
Migrate applications to Microsoft Entra ID authorization with scoped Azure RBAC roles like Storage Blob Data Reader
Generate a single long-lived SAS token and distribute it to all applications instead
Disable the storage account firewall so key-based requests are more reliable
questions.explanation: Current Microsoft guidance is to move away from account keys toward Microsoft Entra ID authorization, enabling scoped, auditable, per-identity RBAC roles instead of one all-or-nothing shared secret. Frequent key rotation reduces the exposure window but keeps the same all-or-nothing risk, and a long-lived shared SAS token has a similar unscoped-sharing problem.

questions.question: A Key Vault currently uses the legacy vault access policy model, and the security team wants to move to fine-grained, auditable Azure RBAC role assignments instead. What is true about making this change?
options: Both access models can be enabled and enforced simultaneously for the same vault
RBAC role assignments for Key Vault can only be applied at the subscription level, not the vault itself
Switching to RBAC has no effect on existing access policies, which continue to apply alongside the new roles
Switching the vault to the Azure RBAC permission model replaces the access policy model for authorization decisions on that vault
questions.explanation: A Key Vault uses one authorization model at a time — switching to the RBAC permission model means role assignments now govern access, replacing rather than layering onto the vault's existing access policies. RBAC role assignments for Key Vault can also be scoped down to the vault or individual objects, not just the subscription.

questions.question: Several App Service instances and a set of Azure Functions need to share the same identity and RBAC role assignments, and that identity must persist even if any one of those resources is deleted and redeployed. What should be created?
options: A user-assigned managed identity, attached to each resource
A system-assigned managed identity on each resource individually
A single service principal with a client secret shared across all app settings
A Key Vault access policy shared across the resource group
questions.explanation: A user-assigned managed identity exists as its own resource independent of any single App Service or Function, so it can be attached to many resources and survives any one of them being deleted and redeployed. A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource's lifecycle and cannot be shared this way.

questions.question: An AKS administrator wants to prevent any pod from being scheduled with privileged container settings across the entire cluster, regardless of which namespace deploys it. Which control should be applied?
options: A Kubernetes network policy restricting which pods can establish network connections to each other
An NSG applied to the AKS subnet, filtering inbound and outbound traffic by IP and port
The Azure Policy add-on for AKS, enforcing a policy that disallows privileged containers
A managed identity assigned to the AKS node pool, used to authenticate to other Azure resources
questions.explanation: Azure Policy's AKS add-on can enforce cluster-wide admission control over what pod configurations, like privileged containers, are allowed to be scheduled at all. A network policy only governs traffic between pods that are already running, not what configurations are permitted in the first place, an NSG filters network traffic rather than pod scheduling, and a node pool's managed identity is unrelated to admission control.

questions.question: A VM's disks already benefit from server-side encryption with platform-managed keys by default. A new requirement demands that the VM's temporary disk and in-memory caches also be encrypted, without configuring BitLocker or DM-Crypt inside the guest OS. Which feature should be enabled?
options: Encryption at host
Azure Disk Encryption (ADE)
Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)
Always Encrypted
questions.explanation: Encryption at host specifically extends encryption to temporary disks and caches at the host level, which default server-side encryption of managed disks does not cover. Azure Disk Encryption instead uses guest-OS-level BitLocker/DM-Crypt, which this requirement explicitly avoids, and TDE/Always Encrypted are SQL-specific features unrelated to VM disk or cache encryption.

questions.question: An App Service application must not only serve traffic over HTTPS, but also verify the certificate presented by the calling client before accepting a request. Which setting accomplishes the second requirement?
options: Enabling "HTTPS Only" in the TLS/SSL settings
Binding a wildcard certificate to a custom domain
Requiring client certificates (mutual TLS)
Enabling a managed identity on the App Service
questions.explanation: Verifying the calling client's own certificate is mutual TLS (client certificate authentication) — "HTTPS Only" only forces the connection to use TLS, without validating who the client is. A managed identity is about the app authenticating outbound to other services, not validating inbound callers.

questions.question: A team deploys an agent in Microsoft Foundry that only needs to read from one specific document index and call a single downstream pricing API. What approach best follows least-privilege practice for this agent?
options: Grant the agent's own identity permissions scoped only to that document index and that one pricing API
Grant the agent the same broad permissions as the development team building it, to avoid future permission requests
Have the agent authenticate using the developer's personal credentials for simplicity
Grant the agent Owner-equivalent access at the subscription level so it can self-provision what it needs
questions.explanation: Least privilege for an agent identity means scoping its permissions to exactly the data source and API it needs, nothing more — broad or borrowed developer-level access turns a single prompt injection or jailbreak against that one agent into a much larger compromise than the agent's actual task requires.

questions.question: A security team wants an agent registered under Microsoft Entra Agent ID to be blocked from authenticating unless it is calling from an approved application and a trusted network location. Which feature should be applied to the agent identity?
options: Azure Policy assigned at the resource group scope
A network security group rule on the agent's hosting subnet
A Conditional Access policy scoped to that agent identity
A Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance standard
questions.explanation: Conditional Access can be scoped to agent identities under Entra Agent ID the same way it targets user identities, evaluating conditions like calling application and network location before granting authentication. An NSG rule or Azure Policy governs network traffic or resource configuration, not identity-level sign-in conditions.

questions.question: Microsoft Defender XDR flags an agent identity as potentially compromised. Before remediating, the security team wants to know every data source, API, and downstream agent that identity could have reached. What capability provides this?
options: Secure Score for the subscription
Blast radius analysis for the agent identity
A Sentinel workbook showing VM performance metrics
The regulatory compliance dashboard
questions.explanation: Blast radius analysis is built specifically to map out everything a flagged agent identity could reach, so containment and cleanup can be scoped accurately. Secure Score and the compliance dashboard reflect general posture and standards conformance, not a specific identity's reachable scope, and a VM performance workbook is unrelated.

questions.question: An organization deploys Azure API Management as an AI Gateway in front of several Microsoft Foundry agents. What does this most directly provide?
options: A central point to enforce authentication, rate limiting, and logging for all traffic reaching the Foundry agents
Automatic encryption of the agents' training data at rest, replacing the need for platform-managed disk encryption
A full replacement for Conditional Access on the agents' identities, since the gateway already evaluates sign-in risk
A significant reduction in prompt injection risk through built-in content filtering rules applied to every request
questions.explanation: An AI Gateway built on Azure API Management centralizes cross-cutting controls — authentication, quotas/rate limiting, and logging — in front of the Foundry agents, so those policies do not have to be reimplemented per agent. It does not itself encrypt training data, replace Conditional Access, or guarantee prompt injection is fully eliminated.

questions.question: A Foundry agent is found to occasionally follow malicious instructions hidden inside the content of a document it retrieves and summarizes. Which control is designed to reduce this kind of risk?
options: Increasing the agent's token quota in the AI Gateway
Assigning the agent a system-assigned managed identity instead of a user-assigned one
Configuring agent guardrails in Foundry to filter and constrain inputs, outputs, and permitted actions
Disabling logging for the agent to reduce its attack surface
questions.explanation: Guardrails configured in Foundry are the control meant to constrain what an agent will act on or output, including reducing the impact of instructions smuggled inside retrieved content (prompt injection). Token quotas and identity type do not address that risk, and disabling logging would actually remove visibility needed to detect it.

questions.question: A SharePoint site was shared broadly with 'Everyone' years ago and largely forgotten. After Microsoft 365 Copilot is enabled, employees start finding sensitive content from that site surfaced in Copilot answers they were technically permitted to see, but should not have easily found. What is the most direct root cause?
options: Copilot has its own separate permission model that ignores SharePoint sharing settings
Copilot requires a Defender for Cloud plan to respect existing permissions
Copilot creates new permission grants for any content it summarizes
The underlying overpermissive SharePoint sharing existed before Copilot and is now easier to discover through it
questions.explanation: Copilot does not introduce a new permission model — it inherits and surfaces whatever access already exists. The oversharing risk comes from pre-existing overpermissive sharing that a human might never have stumbled onto manually, which Copilot can now surface far more readily. Remediating the underlying SharePoint permissions is the actual fix.

questions.question: An organization wants to prevent Microsoft 365 Copilot from using content labeled as highly confidential when generating a response, even for a user who otherwise has permission to view that content. Which control fits this requirement?
options: A Conditional Access policy requiring MFA before using Copilot
A Microsoft Purview DLP policy scoped to Microsoft 365 Copilot
A network security group applied to the Copilot service endpoint
Azure Firewall Premium with TLS inspection enabled
questions.explanation: Purview DLP policies can be applied directly to Microsoft 365 Copilot to block it from using or surfacing content matching a sensitive label or information type, even for a user who is otherwise permitted to see the underlying file. Conditional Access, NSGs, and Azure Firewall govern sign-in conditions or network traffic, not what content an AI feature is allowed to draw from.

questions.question: A line-of-business maker builds a custom agent in Copilot Studio and wants prompts and responses evaluated against the organization's security and compliance policies while the agent is running, not just at publish time. What should an admin enable?
options: A PIM eligible assignment for the maker
A Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance standard
Real-time protection for the Copilot Studio agent
A service endpoint on the agent's hosting subnet
questions.explanation: Real-time protection in Copilot Studio evaluates prompts and responses against configured policies as the agent actually runs, which is the ongoing runtime check this scenario asks for. PIM, the compliance dashboard, and a service endpoint address different concerns — privileged role activation, standards conformance, and network reachability — not runtime prompt/response evaluation.

questions.question: An AI agent grounds its answers using a vector index built from a set of confidential internal documents. A security review focuses only on who can chat with the agent, and concludes access is well controlled. What gap does this review most likely miss?
options: Whether the underlying grounding data store itself has its own appropriately scoped access controls
Whether the agent's token quota in the AI Gateway is set too high
Whether the agent has a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity
Whether the chat interface uses TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3
questions.explanation: Restricting who can chat with the agent says nothing about who can directly access the grounding data store (like the vector index) itself — that store is a full sensitive-data asset in its own right and needs its own access controls, independent of the chat interface's access policy.

questions.question: Two different teams are asked why they gave their AI agent its own Entra Agent ID identity instead of just reusing an existing shared service principal that already had broad API access. What is the strongest justification?
options: Entra Agent ID identities are cheaper to license per month than an equivalent number of service principals
A shared service principal's permissions naturally narrow down to least privilege over time as it accumulates usage history
A dedicated agent identity allows actions to be attributed, scoped, and governed to that specific agent rather than blended with everything else the shared principal does
Service principals are reserved for interactive user sign-in flows, while only Entra Agent ID supports unattended automated workloads
questions.explanation: The value of a dedicated agent identity is attribution and scoping — its actions, permissions, and lifecycle can be governed and audited on their own, rather than mixed in with whatever else a broadly-scoped shared service principal is also doing. Service principals are still valid for other automated workloads; that isn't unique to agents, and neither licensing cost nor automatic self-restriction are real properties of either.

questions.question: A subscription's Secure Score is currently 45%, and leadership wants to know what raising it actually represents. What is the most accurate description?
options: A certification that the environment meets every control required by PCI DSS
The proportion of Defender for Cloud's recommended security controls, weighted by impact, that have actually been implemented
The percentage of resources across the subscription that currently have any Microsoft Defender plan enabled
A rolling measure of how many security alerts were triaged and resolved by the SOC in the last 30 days
questions.explanation: Secure Score reflects how many weighted security recommendations have been remediated, as a general best-practice prioritization measure. It is not a certification against any specific named regulatory standard — that mapping is what the separate regulatory compliance dashboard provides.

questions.question: A company wants Defender for Cloud to scan its Azure SQL databases for outdated permissions and misconfigurations, and also alert on anomalous access patterns that could indicate an active attack. Which single Defender plan provides both capabilities?
options: Defender for Storage
Defender for Resource Manager
Defender for Key Vault
Defender for SQL
questions.explanation: Defender for SQL bundles both vulnerability assessment (misconfiguration/permission scanning) and advanced threat protection (anomalous access alerting) under one plan. Defender for Storage, Key Vault, and Resource Manager each protect a different resource type and would not surface SQL database findings.

questions.question: A VM's RDP port is normally closed by Defender for Cloud, and only opens for a specific source IP and time window after an administrator submits and is granted a request through the portal. What is this feature called?
options: Just-in-time (JIT) VM access
Adaptive application controls
Azure Bastion
The regulatory compliance dashboard
questions.explanation: This is exactly JIT VM access — a port is locked down by default and opened temporarily, scoped to a specific requester, source, and duration. Adaptive application controls govern which applications are allowed to run, not network port exposure, and Bastion avoids exposing the port at all rather than opening it temporarily.

questions.question: Defender for Cloud has learned the normal set of applications that run on a group of production VMs and now alerts whenever a process outside that learned allowlist attempts to execute. Which feature is this?
options: Just-in-time VM access
Adaptive application controls
Microsoft Sentinel Fusion
Dynamic Data Masking
questions.explanation: Adaptive application controls use machine learning to build and enforce an allowlist of known-safe applications per VM group. JIT access controls management port exposure rather than application execution, and Fusion/Dynamic Data Masking are unrelated Sentinel and SQL features respectively.

questions.question: An auditor asks whether the organization's Azure environment currently meets the specific technical controls required by ISO 27001, not just Microsoft's general best-practice recommendations. Which Defender for Cloud feature answers that question?
options: Secure Score
Adaptive application controls
The regulatory compliance dashboard, mapped to the ISO 27001 standard
Just-in-time VM access
questions.explanation: The regulatory compliance dashboard specifically maps environment configuration against named standards like ISO 27001, showing pass/fail per control. Secure Score reflects general best practice rather than conformance to any one named regulatory standard.

questions.question: An organization runs workloads on both Azure and AWS and wants both environments' security posture to appear in the same Defender for Cloud recommendations and secure score. What must be configured first for the AWS resources?
options: Onboard the AWS account using Defender for Cloud's native multicloud connector
Deploy Azure Bastion into the AWS VPC to provide portal-based connectivity for the onboarded resources
Enable Azure Firewall Premium for the AWS account to inspect its inbound and outbound traffic
Create an Azure Policy initiative targeting the AWS region to enforce equivalent configuration rules
questions.explanation: Defender for Cloud's native multicloud connectors are the mechanism for onboarding AWS (and GCP) accounts so their resources appear alongside Azure resources in recommendations and secure score. Azure Bastion and Azure Firewall are Azure networking services with no role in cross-cloud onboarding, and Azure Policy alone does not extend Defender for Cloud visibility into another cloud provider.

questions.question: A SOC wants an automated response that immediately disables a user's account in Microsoft Entra ID the moment a specific Sentinel analytics rule fires, without a human taking manual action. What should they build?
options: A Sentinel hunting query scheduled to run every 5 minutes, which raises a bookmark for an analyst to review
A Log Analytics saved search that an analyst re-runs manually each shift to check for the pattern
An Azure Monitor action group emailing the SOC team so a person can disable the account by hand
A Sentinel playbook (Logic App) triggered automatically from the analytics rule
questions.explanation: A playbook triggered from the analytics rule is exactly Sentinel's SOAR capability — it can automatically take an action like disabling an account, with no human step in between. An action group can only notify people (email, SMS, webhook) rather than directly executing an identity-management action on its own.

questions.question: A Sentinel analyst notices two unrelated low-severity alerts — an unusual sign-in location and, separately, an unusual resource deployment — that individually would not warrant escalation, but together strongly suggest a multi-stage attack. Which Sentinel capability is designed to surface that kind of combined pattern automatically?
options: A scheduled analytics rule querying a single data source
Fusion correlation
A basic hunting bookmark
A Log Analytics workspace retention policy
questions.explanation: Fusion is built specifically to use machine learning to correlate multiple lower-fidelity signals across different sources into one higher-confidence incident. A single scheduled rule against one data source would not naturally connect two unrelated low-severity signals from different sources the way Fusion does.

questions.question: An analyst wants to proactively search historical log data in Sentinel for signs of a specific attacker technique, even though no analytics rule has fired and no incident currently exists. What is this activity called?
options: Incident triage
Playbook execution
Threat hunting
Workbook rendering
questions.explanation: Proactively searching for evidence of compromise before any rule has triggered an incident is threat hunting. Incident triage responds to an incident that already exists, and workbooks/playbooks are visualization and automation tools, not the proactive search activity itself.

questions.question: A company enables Microsoft Sentinel on a Log Analytics workspace that already collects Azure Activity Log and VM performance data from Azure Monitor. What happens to that existing data with respect to Sentinel?
options: Nothing changes automatically — Sentinel requires its own separate, dedicated workspace and cannot read data already collected by Azure Monitor
The existing data must first be manually exported to a storage account and then re-imported into Sentinel's own workspace
Sentinel creates a duplicate copy of the existing data in a new storage account so it has an independent copy to query
That existing data becomes available to Sentinel's analytics rules and hunting queries, since Sentinel is built directly on the Log Analytics workspace
questions.explanation: Sentinel does not maintain a separate log store — it operates directly on a Log Analytics workspace, so data already being collected there is immediately queryable by Sentinel's analytics rules and hunting queries once Sentinel is enabled on that workspace.

questions.question: A team defines an Azure Monitor alert rule for high CPU usage on a set of VMs, and wants any future change to on-call notification recipients to require editing only one place, not every alert rule that references it. What should hold the list of notification recipients?
options: An action group, referenced by the alert rule
A Sentinel playbook
A separate alert rule condition for each recipient
A Log Analytics saved search
questions.explanation: Action groups decouple the "who/how to notify" step from the alert condition itself, so updating notification recipients in one action group automatically applies to every alert rule referencing it. Embedding recipients directly per alert rule would instead require updating each rule individually.

questions.question: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management can manage just-in-time activation for both Azure RBAC roles and Microsoft Entra directory roles.
questions.explanation: PIM covers both role types — Azure resource RBAC roles and Entra ID directory roles like Global Administrator — under the same eligible/active assignment model.

questions.question: Holding the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID automatically grants Owner permissions on every Azure subscription in the tenant.
questions.explanation: Entra ID directory roles and Azure RBAC roles are separate authorization systems. A Global Administrator must explicitly elevate access to gain Azure RBAC permissions across subscriptions — it is not automatic.

questions.question: A user-assigned managed identity can be attached to multiple Azure resources and persists even if one of those resources is deleted.
questions.explanation: Unlike a system-assigned identity, a user-assigned managed identity is its own standalone resource, shareable across multiple resources and independent of any one resource's lifecycle.

questions.question: Continuous Access Evaluation only takes effect the next time a user's token naturally expires, with no ability to revoke access sooner.
questions.explanation: That is the opposite of CAE's purpose — it pushes critical event signals (like an account being disabled) to CAE-enabled services in near real time, revoking a token well before its natural expiration rather than waiting for it.

questions.question: An ExpressRoute circuit encrypts all traffic by default because it does not traverse the public internet.
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute is private but not encrypted by default; achieving encryption requires adding IPsec VPN over ExpressRoute or MACsec.

questions.question: Azure Firewall Standard can filter traffic using FQDN rules and threat intelligence, but cannot perform TLS inspection or intrusion detection and prevention (IDPS).
questions.explanation: TLS inspection and IDPS are Premium-tier-only capabilities. Standard is limited to L3-L7 filtering, FQDN filtering, and threat intelligence-based filtering.

questions.question: Dynamic Data Masking changes how sensitive data is physically stored in an Azure SQL database, encrypting it at the byte level.
questions.explanation: Dynamic Data Masking only obscures values shown in query results to non-privileged users — the underlying stored data is unchanged and unencrypted by this feature specifically.

questions.question: Switching an Azure Key Vault to the Azure RBAC permission model replaces its existing vault access policies for authorization decisions.
questions.explanation: A vault uses one authorization model at a time. Switching to the RBAC permission model means role assignments now govern access, replacing rather than supplementing the legacy access policies.

questions.question: Server-side encryption (SSE) of Azure managed disks with platform-managed keys is enabled by default, without requiring any guest OS configuration.
questions.explanation: SSE is on by default for all managed disks using platform-managed keys, applied transparently outside the guest OS — Azure Disk Encryption is a separate, optional layer for guest-OS-level encryption on top of this.

questions.question: Microsoft Entra Agent ID lets an AI agent's actions be authenticated, authorized, and audited under its own identity, separate from the human user or developer who created it.
questions.explanation: That is the core purpose of Entra Agent ID — giving an agent its own individually identifiable, governed identity rather than blending its actions into a human user's or a generic shared service principal's identity.

questions.question: Deploying an AI Gateway with Azure API Management in front of Microsoft Foundry agents removes the need to apply Conditional Access to those agents' identities.
questions.explanation: An AI Gateway centralizes traffic-level controls like authentication enforcement, rate limiting, and logging — it does not replace identity-level Conditional Access policies applied to the agent identities themselves; the two are complementary layers, not substitutes.

questions.question: Microsoft Purview DLP policies can be applied to Microsoft 365 Copilot to block it from using sensitive labeled content in a response, even for a user who has permission to view the underlying file.
questions.explanation: Purview DLP for Microsoft 365 Copilot can restrict AI-generated exposure of sensitive content independently of the user's underlying file permissions, closing a gap that content access permissions alone do not cover.

questions.question: Blast radius analysis for a compromised agent identity in Defender XDR is limited to showing only the single resource the agent's role assignment directly names.
questions.explanation: Blast radius analysis is meant to map everything the agent identity could actually reach or had recently accessed — including downstream APIs, data sources, and other agents it can invoke — not just the one resource literally named in its role assignment.

questions.question: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Secure Score certifies that an environment is compliant with a specific regulatory standard such as PCI DSS.
questions.explanation: Secure Score reflects adherence to general best-practice recommendations, weighted by impact — it is not a certification against any named regulatory standard. That mapping is what the regulatory compliance dashboard provides instead.

questions.question: Just-in-time VM access reduces exposure of management ports like RDP and SSH by keeping them closed until a specific, approved, time-limited request opens them.
questions.explanation: That is exactly how JIT VM access works — ports stay locked down by default and open temporarily only for an approved requester, source IP, and time window.

questions.question: Microsoft Sentinel maintains its own independent data store, separate from any Log Analytics workspace.
questions.explanation: Sentinel is built directly on top of a Log Analytics workspace and has no separate store of its own — enabling Sentinel on a workspace makes its existing log data immediately available to Sentinel's analytics rules and hunting queries.

questions.question: A Sentinel playbook can be triggered automatically by an analytics rule to take an automated remediation action without human intervention.
questions.explanation: Playbooks are Logic Apps that can be set to trigger automatically from an analytics rule or incident, enabling automated response (SOAR) without requiring a person to manually act.

questions.question: Onboarding an AWS account to Defender for Cloud's native multicloud connector allows AWS resources to appear in the same recommendations and secure score as Azure resources.
questions.explanation: Defender for Cloud's native multicloud connectors extend the same recommendations, secure score, and applicable Defender plans to onboarded AWS (and GCP) resources alongside Azure ones.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Microsoft Entra Conditional Access? (Choose two.)
options: It can block network traffic to a specific port on a VM
It can require a compliant or hybrid-joined device before granting access
It replaces the need for Azure RBAC role assignments entirely
It evaluates conditions like user, group, location, and device platform to decide whether to apply grant or session controls
questions.explanation: Conditional Access evaluates sign-in conditions (user, group, location, device platform, risk) and can require a compliant or hybrid-joined device as a grant control. It has nothing to do with network port-level traffic filtering, which is an NSG/firewall function, and it does not replace Azure RBAC, which governs a separate set of resource-permission decisions.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about cross-tenant access settings and workload identity federation? (Choose two.)
options: Cross-tenant access settings control how much a tenant trusts another tenant's MFA and device claims for B2B collaboration
Workload identity federation requires storing a long-lived client secret for the external workload
Workload identity federation lets an external identity provider's token be exchanged for an Entra ID token without a stored secret
Cross-tenant access settings apply only to workload identities, never to human B2B users
questions.explanation: Cross-tenant access settings govern the trust extended to another tenant's users and their MFA/device claims for B2B collaboration, while workload identity federation is specifically the credential-free way for an external workload's token to be exchanged for an Entra ID token. It does not require a stored secret — that is the point of federation — and cross-tenant access settings are about human B2B trust, not workload identities.

questions.question: Which two of the following are true about Azure Bastion? (Choose two.)
options: It provides RDP/SSH connectivity through the Azure portal without requiring a public IP on the target VM
It requires each target VM to have a public IP address for Bastion to connect to it
It is deployed into a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet
It performs TLS inspection of encrypted web traffic
questions.explanation: Bastion's core value is portal-based RDP/SSH without the target VM needing a public IP at all, and it requires its own dedicated AzureBastionSubnet in the VNet. It does not require target VMs to have public IPs, and TLS inspection of web traffic is an Azure Firewall Premium capability, unrelated to Bastion.

questions.question: Which two of the following correctly describe DDoS Protection Standard versus Basic? (Choose two.)
options: Basic must be manually enabled per virtual network before it provides any protection
Basic and Standard provide identical attack analytics and metrics
Standard adds tuned, resource-specific mitigation policies at the virtual network level
Standard provides cost protection and access to a rapid response team during an attack
questions.explanation: Standard's distinguishing features are tuned mitigation policies applied at the VNet level, plus cost protection and rapid response support during an active attack.
